messages.content: I want to design distributed training recovery that keeps optimizer progress and data progress consistent when failures occur or worker membership changes. What should the design guarantee?

The central guarantee is that a recovered execution matches the optimizer-update and sample-consumption histories of a failure-free execution. That requirement applies even if the failure happens during resharding. Separately, supporting recovery may add at most 5% to failure-free step latency compared with identical training without recovery support.
Why describe optimizer updates and sample consumption together rather than treating them as separate recovery concerns?

Because consistency concerns their relationship. Preserving optimizer progress while losing track of data progress would not establish that the recovered run followed the intended training history. The converse is also true: preserving a record of sample consumption would not suffice if optimizer updates after recovery no longer matched the failure-free history. The goal covers both histories, not just one of them.
Does matching the history mean that it is enough to end up with the same number of updates and consumed samples?

No. Counts alone are weaker than matching histories. Two executions could have the same counts yet differ in which updates occurred or how sample consumption progressed. The requirement is about the optimizer-update and sample-consumption histories of the recovered execution matching those of a failure-free execution, not merely about matching totals at the end.
How should I understand that guarantee when worker membership changes?

A membership change is one of the situations the recovery design must handle without breaking consistency between optimizer and data progress. The workers involved may change, but that change cannot be an excuse for the recovered execution’s optimizer-update or sample-consumption history to diverge from the failure-free history. The goal does not prescribe a particular way to redistribute work or represent that progress.
And a failure during resharding is explicitly included, right?

Yes. The guarantee explicitly includes failures during resharding. It is not limited to failures that happen before resharding begins or after it finishes. Recovery from a failure in that interval must still yield matching optimizer-update and sample-consumption histories.
Could I describe that as making the resharding interval a special exception to the history requirement?

No; it is specifically called out as a case where the history requirement still applies. Resharding can change how work is distributed among workers, but the stated goal does not relax the consistency requirement while that change is under way.
Suppose an implementation restores optimizer progress but cannot establish where sample consumption stands. Has it met the goal?

Not on that information alone. The goal requires matching both histories. If data progress is uncertain, restoring optimizer progress by itself does not establish that sample consumption after recovery matches the failure-free execution. Likewise, knowing the data position alone would not establish that optimizer updates match.
Is the objective only that the final trained result look similar?

No. Similarity of a final result would not, by itself, demonstrate the stated property. The objective is expressed in terms of the execution histories: optimizer updates and sample consumption must match the failure-free case, including across failures and membership changes.
What exactly is the performance comparison?

Compare failure-free step latency for identical training with recovery support against failure-free step latency for that training without recovery support. The added latency may be at most 5%. Expressed as a bound, recovery-supported failure-free step latency must be no more than 1.05 times the comparison latency.
So the 5% figure is a bound on how long recovery itself can take after a failure?

No. The stated 5% limit concerns failure-free step latency: the overhead of having recovery support during normal, failure-free training. It does not specify a maximum duration for recovery after a failure.
Why specify identical training in that comparison?

It keeps the comparison focused on the cost of recovery support. The baseline is the same training without that support, rather than a different training workload. The goal gives the 5% limit for that comparison; it does not supply a measurement method or particular latency figures.
Would it be accurate to say the design has both a correctness condition and an overhead condition?

Yes. The correctness condition is matching failure-free optimizer-update and sample-consumption histories after recovery, including when failure occurs during resharding. The overhead condition is that recovery support adds at most 5% to failure-free step latency relative to identical training without recovery support. Satisfying only one would not satisfy the full goal.
Does this goal already choose a recovery mechanism?

No. It states the behavior the design must preserve and the latency limit it must respect. It does not select a checkpointing scheme, a coordination method, or a way to carry progress across a membership change. Any proposed mechanism would have to be evaluated against the two stated conditions.
When discussing a proposed design, what question would keep us focused on the progress-consistency requirement?

Ask whether, after each relevant failure or membership change—including a failure during resharding—the resulting optimizer-update history and sample-consumption history match those of a failure-free execution. That keeps the focus on the observable requirement without assuming a particular implementation.
And the corresponding question for normal training overhead?

Ask whether enabling recovery support increases failure-free step latency by no more than 5% relative to identical training without recovery support. That is a separate check from whether recovery preserves the two histories.
For this recovery design, I propose deterministic sample IDs and reductions, pipelined durable step journals, checkpoint replay, and epoch-fenced atomic resharding. How do those pieces fit together?

They address different parts of the consistency problem. Deterministic sample IDs make the identity of consumed samples reproducible, while deterministic reductions address reproducibility of the computation that feeds optimizer updates. Durable step journals provide a persistent account of step progress; pipelining is intended to limit their effect on normal step latency. Checkpoint replay provides a way to resume from saved state, and epoch-fenced atomic resharding addresses the transition when worker membership or data placement changes. Together, they form a proposed approach to preserving both histories, not evidence yet that either the history requirement or the 5% latency bound is met.
What does a deterministic sample ID contribute that an ordinary count of consumed samples would not?

A count says how many samples have been consumed, but not which samples they were. Deterministic IDs give samples stable identities that can be referred to across an interruption or a change in workers. That makes it possible to reason about whether recovery continues the intended sample-consumption history rather than merely reaching the same count. The proposal does not, by itself, specify how IDs are assigned or recorded.
Why include deterministic reductions as a separate piece?

Stable sample identities address the data side, but they do not alone make an optimizer update reproducible. A reduction combines contributions used in computation; if its result can vary with execution circumstances, replaying the same identified samples may not reproduce the same update. Deterministic reductions are proposed to make that part of the computation reproducible as well. The proposal names the property without specifying a reduction algorithm.
So are deterministic sample IDs and deterministic reductions enough to handle recovery?

No. They help define and reproduce what the training computation should do, but they do not alone establish which progress was durably retained at a failure, where to resume, or how to handle a membership transition. The step journals, checkpoint replay, and epoch-fenced atomic resharding are proposed for those other aspects.
What should I take 'durable step journal' to mean here?

At the level stated in the proposal, it means a persistent record associated with training-step progress, rather than progress known only to a running worker. Its role is to make recovery reasoning possible after volatile state is lost. The proposal does not specify the journal’s fields, storage system, or exact point at which a step is considered recorded.
And what is gained by pipelining those journals?

Pipelining is an approach to overlapping journal-related work with other training work rather than putting all of that work directly on the step’s critical path. That is relevant to the requirement that recovery support add at most 5% to failure-free step latency compared with identical training without recovery support. It is a performance motivation, not a measured result: the proposal alone does not establish that the bound is achieved.
Could pipelining just mean moving a journal write later, regardless of what happens if a failure intervenes?

That would be an unsafe interpretation of the proposal’s purpose. Pipelining has to be reconciled with durable knowledge of progress: a recovered execution still needs a consistent account of optimizer updates and sample consumption. The proposal does not give a specific rule for when a journal entry must become durable, so that rule remains something a concrete design would have to define and assess.
How does checkpoint replay relate to the journal? Are they interchangeable?

They play different conceptual roles. A checkpoint supplies saved state from which execution can resume; replay concerns reproducing subsequent work as needed. A durable step journal concerns persistent step progress and can inform reasoning about that progress. They are complementary elements in this proposal, not interchangeable terms. Exactly how replay consults the journal is not specified here.
If replay starts from a checkpoint, does this proposal already tell us precisely which steps to run again?

No. It proposes checkpoint replay, but it does not identify a checkpoint selection rule, a precise replay boundary, or the contents of the step journal. Those details would matter for showing that replay neither changes the optimizer-update history nor changes the sample-consumption history, but they are not settled by the proposal as stated.
What is the purpose of an epoch fence during resharding?

An epoch fence conceptually separates authority under one worker-membership arrangement from authority under another. Its purpose in this proposal is to keep operations associated with an earlier arrangement from being treated as valid under the new one merely because they arrive late. The proposal does not specify an epoch representation or a particular fencing protocol.
How does making resharding atomic add to that?

Atomic resharding frames the membership and placement transition as one coherent change, rather than allowing different parts of progress to be interpreted under incompatible arrangements. Paired with epoch fencing, it is intended to make the transition well-defined even if a failure occurs during resharding. 'Atomic' states the desired transition property here; it does not prescribe a particular transaction mechanism.
Is the difficult case a failure that happens while that transition is still under way?

That case is explicitly within the recovery goal. The proposed epoch fence and atomic resharding are directed at making the membership transition unambiguous, including when it is interrupted. The requirement remains that recovery match the failure-free optimizer-update and sample-consumption histories; the proposal does not yet demonstrate how every possible interruption satisfies it.
Could deterministic sample IDs alone decide whether work from the earlier membership is still valid?

No. An ID can establish which sample an operation concerns, but it does not by itself establish whether a worker still has authority to contribute that operation after membership changes. That is why the proposal includes an epoch fence alongside deterministic IDs. Identifying work and determining whether work belongs to the active membership arrangement are distinct concerns.
Likewise, does an epoch fence make the reductions deterministic?

No. A fence concerns which membership epoch an operation belongs to; deterministic reductions concern reproducibility of combined computational contributions. Both can matter across a membership change, but one property does not imply the other.
Can you walk through a general failure scenario without assuming an implementation?

Consider an interruption after some training progress and around a change in worker membership. The proposal would use durable step progress and a checkpoint as the basis for recovery, deterministic sample identities and reductions to make the resumed computation reproducible, and an epoch-fenced atomic resharding boundary to distinguish the membership arrangements. That describes the intended roles of the pieces; it does not assert a particular order of operations or establish that a concrete recovered execution matches a failure-free one.
What would need checking to know whether the proposal actually satisfies the consistency goal?

A concrete design would need to show that its journal durability and replay rules yield the same optimizer-update and sample-consumption histories as a failure-free execution. That check must also cover failures during resharding and worker membership changes, where the epoch fence and atomic transition matter. The named techniques suggest how to approach that proof, but naming them is not itself the proof.
Would a correct recovery argument also establish the latency limit?

No. Correctness of the recovered histories and normal-operation overhead are separate questions. Pipelining the durable journals is relevant to overhead, but meeting the at-most-5% increase in failure-free step latency must be assessed against identical training without recovery support. A correctness argument alone cannot establish that comparison.
How should I state the proposal concisely without making it sound like an already validated result?

You could say: 'Use deterministic sample IDs and reductions, pipelined durable step journals, checkpoint replay, and epoch-fenced atomic resharding as the proposed recovery approach. Evaluate whether recovered executions match failure-free optimizer-update and sample-consumption histories, including failures during resharding, while recovery support adds at most 5% to failure-free step latency versus identical training without it.' That keeps the mechanism proposal distinct from the conditions it still has to satisfy.
How can step journals and ownership fences prevent duplicate optimizer updates or duplicate samples when a worker crashes mid-reshard?

They address two different sources of duplication. A durable step journal can help recovery distinguish progress that was already established from work that must be replayed. An ownership fence can prevent work from an earlier worker-membership arrangement from being accepted after ownership changes. To prevent duplicates, a concrete design must make those two decisions consistent: it cannot replay an update or count a sample that is already part of the accepted history, and it cannot accept a late contribution from a worker that no longer owns the work.
Why is a crash during resharding more awkward than a crash at an ordinary point in training?

During resharding, the question of who owns work is itself in transition. A worker may have begun work under one arrangement while recovery proceeds under another. The journal addresses the status of training progress; the fence addresses which arrangement is allowed to contribute. Without a coherent answer to both questions, the same logical work could be attributed to both arrangements.
If a sample has a deterministic ID, wouldn't that alone prevent it from being consumed twice?

The ID lets the system recognize that two references concern the same sample. It does not, by itself, decide whether an attempted use of that sample belongs in the accepted sample-consumption history. In particular, an old owner and a new owner might both present work bearing the same ID. The ownership rule and the recorded progress still have to determine which work, if any, counts.
What is the journal supposed to tell recovery about an interrupted step?

Conceptually, it needs to provide a durable basis for deciding whether that step's progress is already included in the accepted history or needs to be reproduced. The important point is that an interruption must not turn an uncertain step into two accepted optimizer updates, or cause its samples to be counted twice. The proposal does not specify the journal's contents or the precise rule that makes a step final.
Can we simply replay every step that might have been interrupted?

Not without a rule for distinguishing replay from an additional accepted update or additional sample consumption. Re-executing computation may be part of checkpoint replay, but the recovered optimizer-update and sample-consumption histories must still match the failure-free histories. If progress was already accepted before the crash, accepting its replay as new progress would create a duplicate.
What if the worker performed an optimizer update but crashed before its journal entry became durable?

That is exactly the kind of boundary a concrete design must resolve. It cannot assume that the mere act of computing an update tells recovery whether the update belongs in durable, accepted progress. The rules connecting optimizer updates, sample consumption, and journal durability must leave recovery with an unambiguous history. The proposal names durable step journals but does not yet define those rules.
So does the journal have to record every intermediate action?

That does not follow from the question or proposal. What matters for the stated goal is whether the durable information and recovery rules are sufficient to reconstruct the correct optimizer-update and sample-consumption histories. Exactly what is recorded, and at what granularity, remains an implementation question rather than a specified requirement here.
Where does an ownership fence enter if the crashing worker is no longer running?

The concern is not limited to that worker continuing to run. Work begun under the earlier ownership arrangement could still be in flight or could become visible late. A fence distinguishes the authority of the earlier arrangement from that of the new one, so that late work cannot simply be accepted as though ownership had never changed. It also gives recovery a basis for treating the transition as one ownership change rather than two overlapping ones.
Is fencing just another way of saying that the new worker takes over?

No. Takeover describes who will do work next; fencing addresses whether work associated with the previous owner may still be accepted. If takeover occurs while earlier work can also count, there is a duplication risk. The fence is the proposed way to keep authority from overlapping across the membership change.
Suppose both the previous owner and a replacement present the same sample ID. What question should recovery answer?

It should determine whether that sample is already part of the accepted consumption history and which ownership arrangement, if either, is authorized to contribute the work in question. Recognizing the shared ID identifies the potential duplicate; the progress and fencing rules decide what counts. The answer cannot depend only on which contribution arrives first unless a concrete design establishes that such a rule preserves the required histories.
Does a fence by itself tell us whether the old owner's optimizer update was already accepted?

No. A fence can rule out contributions that lack current ownership authority, but it does not by itself reconstruct past accepted optimizer progress. That is why the journal and the ownership boundary have to work together. One concerns the status of progress; the other concerns authority across the resharding transition.
And does the journal alone rule out a late contribution from the old ownership arrangement?

Not necessarily. A journal can help identify progress already established, but it does not automatically establish that a worker submitting later work still has authority after resharding. An ownership fence addresses that separate issue. Neither named component, considered in isolation, proves that duplicates cannot be accepted.
How does atomic resharding affect this explanation?

Atomic resharding is the proposed way to make the ownership transition a coherent boundary. A crash mid-reshard must not leave recovery treating the same work as valid under both the earlier and the new arrangement. The fence marks the ownership distinction, while the journal helps identify which step progress is already accepted. The proposal does not specify the mechanism that makes the transition atomic.
Could we state the core rule as 'either the old owner did it or the new owner does it'?

That captures part of the idea, but it needs a qualification: what matters is which work becomes part of the accepted optimizer-update and sample-consumption histories, not just which worker performed computation. A worker might have computed something before a crash without that computation constituting accepted progress. The recovery rules must settle that distinction consistently with ownership.
So replaying computation and duplicating a sample in the training history are not necessarily the same thing?

Right. Replay can repeat computation as part of reconstructing state. The requirement is that recovery not introduce an extra sample-consumption event or optimizer update into the accepted history. A proposed design must define how replayed work is treated so that repeating computation does not become duplicate progress.
Could the two histories disagree even if duplicate optimizer updates are prevented?

Yes. Preventing an update from counting twice does not by itself ensure that its associated sample consumption is counted correctly. The recovery goal requires both histories to match the failure-free execution. A consistent rule must account for data progress as well as optimizer progress at the interrupted step and across the ownership change.
Does deterministic reduction solve the duplicate-update question?

No. Deterministic reductions help make a repeated computation reproducible, but reproducibility does not decide whether a result should be accepted once, replayed as reconstruction, or rejected as late work from an earlier owner. The journal and ownership boundary address those decisions conceptually.
What's the hardest ambiguity to watch for at the moment of a mid-reshard crash?

Whether a piece of work was accepted under the earlier ownership arrangement, remains to be replayed under a valid arrangement, or is a late contribution that must not count. If recovery cannot distinguish those cases consistently for both optimizer updates and sample consumption, it risks either duplication or a gap in the histories. The proposed journals and fences are meant to make that distinction possible, but their exact coordination is not specified.
How would I phrase a test of this idea without assuming the journal and fence already work?

Ask whether, for a worker crash at any point during resharding, the proposed durable progress rules and ownership fence leave exactly one accepted history of optimizer updates and sample consumption that matches a failure-free execution. In particular, check that work from the former owner cannot count again after replay or takeover, while work not yet accepted is not silently lost. That frames what must be shown rather than declaring it proven.
If a design handles the ordinary crash case, can we infer that it also handles a crash mid-reshard?

No. Mid-reshard failure adds the ownership-transition question to the progress question. The journal may give a way to reason about an interrupted step, but the design must also show that its ownership fence and atomic resharding boundary prevent both ownership arrangements from accepting the same work. That case needs to be covered explicitly.

Here is a hypothesis for the mid-reshard crash case: epoch-fenced step-journal commits and deterministic sample-ID replay preserve identical update hashes and sample-ID sequences across those crashes. Is that a fair way to frame it?

Yes, as a hypothesis rather than an established result. It predicts that, despite a crash during resharding, the recovered execution will have update hashes and an ordered sequence of sample IDs identical to the corresponding failure-free execution. The proposed explanation combines a fence on step-journal commits with deterministic replay of sample IDs; it still needs to be checked.
What does adding an epoch fence to a step-journal commit contribute to the hypothesis?

It ties acceptance of a journal commit to the ownership epoch in which that commit is authorized. Conceptually, that should keep progress from an earlier ownership arrangement from being accepted as new progress after the transition. The hypothesis does not specify how epochs are represented or how commit authority is enforced.
Is that different from simply putting an epoch label on each journal entry?

Potentially. A label identifies the epoch associated with an entry; a fence must also affect whether its commit can be accepted. The hypothesis says *epoch-fenced step-journal commits*, so its intended protection is about commit authority, not merely descriptive labeling. It does not prescribe a particular enforcement mechanism.
Why focus on commits rather than just on what a worker calculated?

Calculation and accepted progress are not necessarily the same thing. Around a crash, a worker might have begun or calculated work whose status must still be resolved. The hypothesis places the fence at step-journal commits so that the accepted record of step progress has a defined ownership boundary. Whether a concrete design actually provides that boundary remains to be shown.
Where does deterministic sample-ID replay enter the picture?

It is the proposed way to make sample consumption reproducible when work is resumed or repeated. If recovery replays from saved progress, deterministic sample IDs give it a basis for reproducing the intended ordered sample-ID sequence rather than selecting samples based on whichever workers happen to be available. That describes the hypothesis’s intended effect, not a proven replay rule.
Does 'identical sample-ID sequences' mean only that the same samples appear somewhere after recovery?

No. A sequence includes order and occurrences. Merely having the same collection of IDs would not establish an identical sample-ID sequence: an ID could appear twice, be missing, or appear in a different position. The hypothesis predicts identity of the sequences across the mid-reshard crash case.
And what exactly is being compared when we say 'identical update hashes'?

The hypothesis proposes comparing the hashes associated with optimizer updates in the recovered and corresponding failure-free executions. If the update hashes are identical in the relevant history, that is a precise proposed observation about update consistency. The hypothesis does not define the hash construction or claim that this comparison has already been performed.
Could matching the number of updates stand in for matching their hashes?

No. Equal counts would not establish that the updates themselves match. The hypothesis specifically predicts identical update hashes, just as it predicts identical sample-ID sequences rather than equal sample counts.
Is the hypothesis making two independent predictions?

It makes two related predictions about the same recovery behavior: update hashes remain identical, and sample-ID sequences remain identical. Both matter because matching the optimizer side alone would leave data progress unaccounted for, while matching sample IDs alone would not establish matching updates.
How does the combination address a worker crashing partway through resharding?

The proposed fence governs which ownership epoch may commit step progress across the transition, while deterministic sample-ID replay is intended to reproduce data progress after an interruption. If they work together as hypothesized, the crash will not cause an extra or missing accepted update, nor an extra, missing, or reordered sample ID relative to the failure-free history. That is the claim to investigate, not a demonstrated outcome.
Could a journal commit from the earlier epoch arrive late and still be harmless?

The hypothesis depends on the epoch fence determining whether such a commit may count. A late arrival cannot be accepted merely because it exists; its authority has to be resolved under the fence. The statement does not tell us what happens to any particular late commit, only the predicted consequence for the resulting update hashes and sample-ID sequence.
What if the replacement worker replays a sample whose ID also appeared in work started by the old worker?

The shared ID would make the potential overlap identifiable, but the important distinction is whether the earlier work was already accepted as progress. The hypothesis predicts that fenced commits and deterministic replay resolve that distinction without creating a duplicate in the accepted sample-ID sequence or a duplicate accepted update. It does not specify the exact rule for that case.
Does deterministic replay mean no computation can ever be repeated?

No. Replay can involve repeating computation. The prediction is about the resulting accepted histories: the sample-ID sequence and update hashes should be identical to the failure-free case. Repeated computation must not turn into an additional accepted sample occurrence or optimizer update.
If the sample-ID sequences match but one update hash differs, would the hypothesis hold?
No. It predicts both identical update hashes and identical sample-ID sequences. A difference in either would fail to support the hypothesis as stated for that comparison.
What about identical update hashes but one sample ID appears twice?
That would also contradict the stated prediction. A duplicate occurrence changes the sample-ID sequence even if the update hashes happen to match. The two observations are deliberately separate.
Does the hypothesis already guarantee consistency for every kind of failure?

No. Its stated scope is crashes during resharding. The broader recovery goal also concerns failures and worker membership changes generally, but this hypothesis specifically proposes what epoch-fenced step-journal commits and deterministic sample-ID replay would preserve across mid-reshard crashes. It should not be presented as an established guarantee for other cases.
Should I say that the hashes and sequences *will* match?

It is better to keep the conditional, investigative framing: 'We hypothesize that epoch-fenced step-journal commits and deterministic sample-ID replay preserve identical update hashes and sample-ID sequences across mid-reshard crashes.' Saying they have been shown to match would turn a hypothesis into a reported result.
Can the hypothesis tell us how much failure-free step latency the recovery design adds?

No. The hypothesis concerns consistency across mid-reshard crashes, expressed through update hashes and sample-ID sequences. It supplies no latency measurement or bound. The separate goal remains that recovery support add at most 5% to failure-free step latency versus identical training without recovery support.
What is the clearest question this hypothesis sets up?

Whether, when a worker crashes during resharding, the recovered execution using epoch-fenced step-journal commits and deterministic sample-ID replay yields update hashes and a sample-ID sequence identical to those of the corresponding failure-free execution. That asks for the specific observations the hypothesis predicts without assuming the answer.
Is it important to check the two observations over the history, rather than only after recovery has finished?

Yes. The stated prediction concerns update hashes and a sample-ID *sequence* across the interruption. Looking only at a final count or final state could miss an extra, missing, or differently ordered event. The comparison needs to capture the histories the hypothesis says are identical; it does not require assuming a particular way of recording them.
So the fence and replay are the proposed cause, and identical hashes and sequences are the predicted outcome?

That is a useful distinction. Epoch-fenced step-journal commits and deterministic sample-ID replay are the proposed means; identical update hashes and sample-ID sequences across mid-reshard crashes are the predicted outcome. The connection between them is precisely what the hypothesis leaves open for verification.

I want to implement fenced commits, then crash workers during the phases of an 8→12-worker reshard and compare update hashes, sample sequences, and p95 step latency against an uninterrupted baseline. Does that plan directly test the mid-reshard concern?

Yes. It puts the proposed commit boundary under the condition of interest—a crash during a worker-membership change—and compares the recovered run with an uninterrupted baseline. Update hashes and sample sequences address whether optimizer and data progress match; p95 step latency provides a performance comparison. This is a plan for a test, not a result.
Why specify the change as 8→12 workers rather than just saying 'a reshard'?

The plan specifies the membership change being exercised: from 8 workers to 12. That makes the planned comparison concrete. It does not, on its own, say that the outcome would generalize to every membership change or every failure.
When I say I'll crash workers during reshard phases, have I already defined exactly when each crash occurs?

No. The plan calls for crashes during the phases of that reshard, but it does not enumerate the phases or fix crash points within them. Those details would have to be defined when carrying out the plan. The important scope stated here is that crashes occur during the 8→12-worker reshard, rather than only before or after it.
What should the update-hash comparison tell me?

It is intended to reveal whether the optimizer updates in a recovered execution match those in the uninterrupted baseline. Comparing hashes over the relevant update history is more informative for that purpose than comparing update counts alone: a count could match even if an update differed. The plan does not specify how the hashes are constructed.
And why compare sample sequences, rather than just total samples consumed?

A sequence comparison can expose a missing, extra, duplicated, or differently ordered sample ID that an equal total would conceal. It tests the data-progress side of the recovery requirement alongside the update-hash comparison. The plan does not specify a recording format for those sequences.
If the update hashes match but the sample sequence differs, what would that mean for this test?

The planned consistency comparison would not show matching histories on both sides. Matching update hashes would address the update observation, but a different sample sequence would fail the sample-progress observation. The recovery goal requires both optimizer-update and sample-consumption histories to match the failure-free execution.
What if the sample sequences match but an update hash differs?

That would leave the update comparison unmatched even though the sample comparison matched. The plan deliberately examines both, so a match on just one is not enough to support the predicted consistency across the crash.
How do fenced commits connect to those comparisons?

Fenced commits are the part to implement before inducing crashes. Their proposed role is to prevent progress associated with the wrong ownership epoch from being accepted across the resharding transition. The hash and sequence comparisons then check the resulting histories against the uninterrupted baseline. The comparison is needed because implementing a fence does not, by itself, demonstrate that duplicates or omissions were prevented.
Does this plan specify how a step-journal commit becomes fenced?

No. It says to implement fenced commits but gives no commit protocol, journal layout, or epoch-enforcement mechanism. Those are design details still to be worked out; the stated test is about what the implementation produces when workers crash during the 8→12-worker reshard.
What does 'uninterrupted baseline' mean in these comparisons?

It is the reference execution without the injected interruption, used to compare update hashes, sample sequences, and p95 step latency with the runs involving crashes. The plan does not further specify how that baseline is configured. In particular, it does not say that the uninterrupted baseline is identical training *without recovery support*.
Why is that distinction about recovery support important for the latency figure?

The broader 5% overhead requirement compares failure-free step latency for identical training with and without recovery support. This plan instead names an uninterrupted baseline for its p95 step-latency comparison. Without more information about that baseline, the planned p95 comparison should not be described as a measurement of the 5% recovery-support overhead.
What does p95 step latency describe here?

It is the 95th-percentile step latency: a way of looking beyond a typical step to slower steps in the measured set. The plan says to compare that quantity against the uninterrupted baseline. It does not provide measured values, an acceptable p95 difference, or a duration limit for recovery after a crash.
Could I treat a small p95 difference as proof that the histories match?

No. Latency describes timing, not which optimizer updates or samples became part of the execution history. The update hashes and sample sequences are the planned consistency observations; p95 step latency is a separate performance observation.
Would a comparison after only one crash point cover the stated plan?

Not fully as phrased. The plan calls for crashes during reshard phases, which implies exercising the transition rather than relying solely on one unspecified crash point. It does not state how many crash trials or which exact points are required, so those particulars should not be inferred.
Does a passing comparison in this 8→12-worker case prove recovery is correct for all failures and membership changes?

No. It would provide evidence for the tested crash conditions during that 8→12-worker reshard. The plan does not claim coverage of every failure point or every membership change. The broader recovery goal remains more general than this particular planned test.
Should I report the comparisons now as though the recovered and uninterrupted runs matched?

No. At this point the node is a plan: implement fenced commits, induce crashes during the 8→12-worker reshard phases, and compare update hashes, sample sequences, and p95 step latency against the uninterrupted baseline. It reports no observed matches or latency measurements.
Then what is the precise question the planned experiment is positioned to answer?

For crashes during the planned 8→12-worker reshard, do the recovered runs with fenced commits produce update hashes and sample sequences matching the uninterrupted baseline, and how does their p95 step latency compare with that baseline? The plan sets up those comparisons without presupposing their results.
For the next activity, run 100 ReshardCrash-8to12 trials with crashes during shard transfer and commit, then compare update hashes and sample IDs against the baseline. What does that cover?

It covers two specified crash windows in an 8→12-worker reshard: shard transfer and commit. Across 100 ReshardCrash-8to12 trials, the intended observations are the update hashes and sample IDs, compared with the baseline. The activity specifies what to run and compare; it does not report results.
Are those 100 trials for each crash window?
